diagnostic_evidence.quote: Therefore, we can solve for $y_{i_1i_2\ldots i_N}$ in \eqref{e:TjYC}, if and only if $t_{1,i_1,i_1} + t_{2,i_2,i_2} + \dots + t_{N,i_N,i_N}\not=0$
has a unique solution $\X\in\CC^{n_1\times n_2}$, if and only if $\sigma(\A_1) \cap \sigma(-\A_2) = \emptyset$

issues.failure_explanation: The nonvanishing of all eigenvalue sums is equivalent to the Kronecker-sum matrix being nonsingular, i.e., to existence of a unique solution for every right-hand side B. It is not equivalent to mere existence of a solution for the given B: if some eigenvalue sum vanishes, a solution still exists for suitable B (e.g., B = 0 gives X = 0), only non-uniquely. The 'if and only if ... have a solution' claim is therefore false as stated; the correct statement is 'a unique solution for all B iff'.

failure_location.quote: Therefore, \eqref{e:sylvesterND} and \eqref{e:TjYC} have a solution if and only if, when taking an eigenvalue of each matrix $\A_j$, their sum is always different from zero

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Restate the condition as: (e:sylvesterND) has a unique solution for every B if and only if no sum of eigenvalues (one from each A_j) vanishes; this is the condition under which the recursion (e:yi1i2iN) is well defined.
issues.overall_effect: The stated solvability characterization is inaccurate; the algorithm's actual precondition (all eigenvalue sums nonzero, so that no division by zero occurs in (e:yi1i2iN)) is a sufficient condition for unique solvability, not a necessary condition for existence.
issues.title: Existence characterization stated as 'iff' is false in the 'only if' direction
issues.why_classification: A one-sentence local restatement fixes the claim; the algorithm and all other results are unaffected.

We explain carefully all the steps, and calculate accurately the computational cost required.

issues.failure_explanation: Each entry of Y needs exactly one division, so the total is n_1...n_N divisions, not n_1...n_N N. Moreover, even with the paper's own summands, (P/2)[5S-N] + (P/2)[5S-3N-2] + PN = P[5S-2N-1] + PN = P[5S-N-1], not P[5S-N+1] (with P = n_1...n_N, S = sum n_j). With the corrected division count the total is P[5S-2N]. The advertised 'accurate' operation count is thus incorrect in its lower-order terms.

Then, the solution $\X(t)$ at a given time satisfies the following $N$-dimensional Sylvester equation

issues.failure_explanation: Theorem theo:evolND only shows that X(t) satisfies (e:sylvesterNDC); this determines X(t) only if the Kronecker sum A_N ⊕ ... ⊕ A_1 is nonsingular, i.e., no sum of eigenvalues (one from each A_j) vanishes. No such hypothesis is stated in the theorem or in the surrounding text, yet the paper claims the computation of X(t) is 'reduced' to the matrix equation and implements it via Algorithm alg:sylvesterND, which divides by the eigenvalue sum. When A is singular (e.g., some A_j has a zero eigenvalue and the others share eigenvalues summing to zero, a common situation for discretized operators), the ODE solution exists but the Sylvester equation has infinitely many solutions and the algorithm divides by zero.

failure_location.quote: reduce the calculation of the solution of \eqref{e:evolND} at any given $t$ to a matrix equation of the form of \eqref{e:sylvesterND}

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Add to Theorem theo:evolND (or the reduction claim) the hypothesis that no sum of eigenvalues of A_1,...,A_N vanishes, so that (e:sylvesterNDC) has a unique solution equal to X(t).
issues.overall_effect: The claimed general reduction of (e:evolND) to (e:sylvesterND) and the evolND implementation are only valid under an unstated nonsingularity assumption on the Kronecker sum of the A_j.
issues.title: Reduction of the ODE solution to a Sylvester equation silently requires the nonsingularity (eigenvalue-sum) condition
issues.why_classification: Adding the standard solvability hypothesis is a local fix; the theorem's argument and the method are otherwise correct and the advertised scope is essentially preserved.
